questions.topic: Roles of government in agricultural development
questions.stem:
(a) Explain five ways in which the government can promote agricultural development in Nigeria. [10 marks]
(b) State four functions of agricultural research institutes. [4 marks]
(c) Name two agricultural research institutes in Nigeria and state the main crop or animal each works on. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
10 marks: (a) Any five explained, 2 marks each: provision of credit/loans at low interest; subsidies on inputs (fertilisers, seeds, agrochemicals); provision of rural infrastructure (roads, electricity, water); funding research and extension services; guaranteed minimum prices/price support; land reform for access to land; provision of storage and processing facilities; irrigation schemes; agricultural education and training; favourable import/export policies
4 marks: (b) Any four, 1 mark each: develop improved crop varieties/animal breeds; develop pest and disease control methods; improve farm practices; produce and distribute improved planting materials; train farmers and extension staff; carry out soil surveys
4 marks: (c) Any two correctly matched, 2 marks each: IAR Zaria - cereals/cotton/groundnut; NRCRI Umudike - root and tuber crops (yam, cassava); CRIN Ibadan - cocoa, kola, coffee, cashew; NIFOR Benin - oil palm, coconut, date palm; RRIN Iyanomo - rubber; NAPRI Shika - livestock; NIFFR New Bussa - freshwater fisheries; NCRI Badeggi - rice and other cereals
questions.explanation: Government promotes agriculture through credit, input subsidies, rural infrastructure, research and extension, price support, land reform, storage and irrigation. Research institutes breed improved varieties, develop pest control and train farmers. Examples include NRCRI Umudike (root crops), CRIN Ibadan (cocoa) and NIFOR (oil palm).

questions.topic: Role of non-governmental organizations in agricultural development
questions.stem:

(b) Explain five ways in which NGOs contribute to agricultural development in rural communities. [10 marks]
(c) State three problems that limit the effectiveness of NGOs in agricultural development. [3 marks]
(d) Name three examples of NGOs or international bodies that support agriculture in Nigeria. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) A private, non-profit organisation, independent of government, that works to improve the welfare of people or communities
10 marks: (b) Any five explained, 2 marks each: training farmers in improved practices; provision of credit/micro-loans; supply of improved inputs and livestock; formation and strengthening of farmers' groups/co-operatives; provision of rural infrastructure such as wells and storage; support for women and youth in agriculture; promotion of conservation and sustainable practices; linking farmers to markets
3 marks: (c) Any three, 1 mark each: inadequate funds; dependence on foreign donors; poor co-operation from communities; insecurity; government bureaucracy; poor rural access; short project life
3 marks: (d) Any three, 1 mark each: Heifer International; Sasakawa Africa Association; FAO (UN agency); IFAD; Oxfam; Catholic Relief Services; Self Help Africa; One Acre Fund (any recognised body)
questions.explanation: An NGO is a private, non-profit organisation working for community welfare. NGOs train farmers, give micro-credit, supply inputs, organise co-operatives, build rural facilities, support women and link farmers to markets. They are limited by funding, insecurity and poor access. Examples include Heifer International, Sasakawa Africa Association and IFAD.

questions.topic: Factors affecting land availability for agricultural purpose

(b) Suggest three ways of making more land available for farming. [3 marks]
(c) State three effects of land shortage on agricultural production. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
12 marks: (a) Any six explained, 2 marks each: population pressure/urbanisation; land tenure system (communal, inheritance and fragmentation); industrial and infrastructural development (roads, airports); soil erosion; desert encroachment; flooding/waterlogging; mining and oil exploration; topography (steep slopes, rocky areas); low soil fertility; government acquisition for reserves; insecurity/communal conflicts
3 marks: (b) Any three, 1 mark each: land reform/Land Use Act enforcement; reclamation of swamps by drainage; irrigation of arid land; erosion control; afforestation/stopping desert spread; consolidation of fragmented plots; terracing of slopes
3 marks: (c) Any three, 1 mark each: small farm sizes; low output; difficulty in mechanising; continuous cropping reducing fertility; land disputes; increase in land rent
questions.explanation: Land for farming is reduced by population growth and urbanisation, land tenure and fragmentation, infrastructure, erosion, desertification, flooding, mining, steep topography and insecurity. Reclamation, irrigation, erosion control and land reform increase available land. Land shortage causes small, unmechanisable farms and low output.

questions.stem:
(a) What is farm drainage? [2 marks]
(b) Describe three methods of draining waterlogged farmland. [9 marks]
(c) State four effects of poor drainage on crops and soil. [4 marks]
(d) Name three crops that tolerate waterlogged conditions. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) The removal of excess water from the soil surface or root zone of farmland
3 marks: (b) Surface (open ditch) drainage: open channels/ditches dug across or around the field to carry away excess surface water
3 marks: (b) Sub-surface (tile/pipe) drainage: perforated pipes or tiles laid in trenches below the surface and covered with gravel to collect and remove water
3 marks: (b) Any one other described: mole drainage (channels made by a mole plough); French drains (trenches filled with stones); pumping; cambered beds/ridges; planting water-loving trees (biological drainage)
4 marks: (c) Any four, 1 mark each: poor aeration/root suffocation; denitrification and loss of nitrogen; accumulation of toxic substances; cold soil delays germination; encourages root diseases; difficult tillage; leaching/salt accumulation; poor root development
3 marks: (d) Any three, 1 mark each: swamp rice; sugar cane; cocoyam (taro); water leaf; raffia palm
questions.explanation: Drainage removes excess water. Open ditches remove surface water; tile or pipe drains remove water from the root zone; mole drains, French drains and pumping are also used. Waterlogging causes poor aeration, denitrification, toxicity, diseases and difficult tillage. Rice, sugar cane and taro tolerate wet soils.

questions.stem:
(a) Define agricultural pollution. [2 marks]
(b) Explain how each of the following farm practices can cause pollution: (i) excessive use of fertilisers; (ii) indiscriminate use of pesticides; (iii) bush burning; (iv) poor disposal of livestock waste. [8 marks]
(c) Suggest four ways of reducing pollution arising from farming. [4 marks]
(d) State four effects of agricultural pollution on human health. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) The contamination of land, water or air with harmful substances arising from agricultural activities
2 marks: (b)(i) Excess nitrates and phosphates leach or run off into water bodies, causing eutrophication and contaminating drinking water
2 marks: (b)(ii) Residues remain in soil, crops and water; kill beneficial organisms; accumulate in food chains
2 marks: (b)(iii) Releases smoke, carbon dioxide and particles into the air; destroys soil organisms and organic matter
2 marks: (b)(iv) Dung and urine washed into streams contaminate water with pathogens and nutrients; offensive odour/ammonia in air
4 marks: (c) Any four, 1 mark each: use correct rates and timing of fertilisers; integrated pest management/biological control; composting/biogas from animal waste; avoid bush burning (use controlled burning); buffer strips near water bodies; proper disposal of chemical containers; training of farmers
4 marks: (d) Any four, 1 mark each: poisoning from pesticide residues; respiratory problems from smoke; water-borne diseases; cancers; skin and eye irritation; methaemoglobinaemia from nitrates in water
questions.explanation: Agricultural pollution is contamination of land, water and air by farming. Excess fertilisers cause eutrophication; pesticides leave toxic residues; bush burning releases smoke; untreated animal waste contaminates water. Correct application, IPM, composting, buffer strips and training reduce it. Health effects include poisoning, respiratory illness and water-borne disease.

questions.stem:
(a) State six routine maintenance practices that should be carried out on a farm tractor. [6 marks]
(b) State four safety precautions a tractor operator should observe. [4 marks]
(c) Explain four maintenance practices for simple farm tools such as hoes and cutlasses. [8 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
6 marks: (a) Any six, 1 mark each: check engine oil level daily; check water/coolant in radiator; check tyre pressure; grease moving parts; clean or replace air filter; check battery water and terminals; check fuel level and filters; check fan belt tension; change engine oil at recommended intervals; tighten loose bolts
4 marks: (b) Any four, 1 mark each: only trained persons should operate it; do not carry passengers; switch off the engine before refuelling or repairs; avoid steep slopes/drive slowly on rough ground; keep children away; wear protective clothing; disengage PTO when not in use
8 marks: (c) Any four explained, 2 marks each: clean off soil and plant sap after use to prevent rust; oil or grease metal parts before storage; sharpen blunt edges with a file; tighten or replace loose/broken handles; store in a dry, safe place/tool shed; paint metal parts to prevent rusting; use tools only for their intended purpose
questions.explanation: Tractor maintenance includes daily checks of oil, coolant, tyres, battery, filters and greasing. Operators must be trained, carry no passengers, switch off before refuelling and avoid steep slopes. Simple tools should be cleaned, oiled, sharpened, fitted with sound handles and stored dry.

questions.stem:
(a) Name five sources of farm power. [5 marks]
(b) State two advantages and two disadvantages of each of the following sources of farm power: (i) human power; (ii) animal power; (iii) mechanical (tractor) power. [12 marks]
(c) Name one farm operation that can be powered by wind. [1 mark]
questions.markingGuide:
5 marks: (a) Any five, 1 mark each: human; animal; mechanical (engines/tractors); electrical; solar; wind; water (hydro); biogas
2 marks: (b)(i) Human advantages, any two: cheap/readily available; suited to small plots; flexible for delicate operations
2 marks: (b)(i) Human disadvantages, any two: tiring and slow; low output; unsuitable for large farms; affected by health/fatigue
2 marks: (b)(ii) Animal advantages, any two: stronger than humans; cheaper than tractors; dung used as manure; reproduces itself
2 marks: (b)(ii) Animal disadvantages, any two: animals need feeding and care; affected by diseases (e.g. trypanosomiasis); slow compared with tractors; training needed
2 marks: (b)(iii) Mechanical advantages, any two: fast; covers large areas; reduces drudgery; performs many operations
2 marks: (b)(iii) Mechanical disadvantages, any two: expensive to buy and maintain; needs skilled operators; causes soil compaction; spare parts scarce; unsuitable for small fragmented plots
1 mark: (c) Pumping water / grinding grain / winnowing
questions.explanation: Farm power comes from humans, animals, engines, electricity, sun, wind, water and biogas. Human power is cheap but slow; animal power is stronger and cheaper than tractors but animals need care and suffer disease; tractors are fast but costly and need skill. Wind can pump water or grind grain.

questions.stem:
(a) What is a farmstead? [2 marks]
(b) Explain five factors that should be considered when siting a farmstead. [10 marks]
(c) State the most suitable location, in relation to the farmhouse, of each of the following, giving a reason: (i) pig pen; (ii) machinery shed; (iii) feed store. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) The part of a farm where the farmhouse and other farm buildings such as stores, animal pens and sheds are located
10 marks: (b) Any five explained, 2 marks each: nearness to good road for easy transport; well-drained, gently sloping land to avoid flooding; availability of water supply; direction of prevailing wind (odour away from house); security; nearness to fields to reduce travelling; availability of electricity; soil stability for building; room for future expansion; avoid fertile cropland for buildings
2 marks: (c)(i) Pig pen: away from the farmhouse and downwind, because of odour and flies (1 mark location, 1 mark reason)
2 marks: (c)(ii) Machinery shed: near the farm road/entrance and close to the farmhouse, for easy movement of machines and security
2 marks: (c)(iii) Feed store: close to the animal houses, to reduce labour in carrying feed; dry and raised to protect feed
questions.explanation: The farmstead is where the farmhouse and buildings are grouped. It should be accessible, well drained, near water and fields, secure, sited with regard to wind, and allow expansion. Pig pens go downwind away from the house; machinery sheds near the road and house; feed stores beside animal houses.

questions.stem:
(a) Distinguish between natural pasture and artificial (sown) pasture. [4 marks]
(b) Name two grasses and two legumes suitable for establishing pasture in Nigeria. [4 marks]
(c) Describe four steps in the establishment of an artificial pasture. [8 marks]
(d) State two reasons for including legumes in a pasture. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Natural pasture: grassland that grows on its own without being planted by man; contains mixed, often low-quality species
2 marks: (a) Artificial pasture: deliberately established by sowing selected grasses and/or legumes, often fertilised and managed
2 marks: (b) Grasses, any two: Panicum maximum (Guinea grass); Pennisetum purpureum (elephant grass); Andropogon gayanus (gamba grass); Cynodon (star grass); Brachiaria; Chloris gayana
2 marks: (b) Legumes, any two: Centrosema pubescens; Stylosanthes (stylo); Calopogonium mucunoides; Pueraria phaseoloides; Lablab purpureus; Leucaena
8 marks: (c) Any four steps described, 2 marks each: site selection (water, soil, accessibility); land clearing and ploughing/harrowing to a fine tilth; selection of suitable grass-legume mixture; sowing seed (broadcast or drill) or planting splits/cuttings at the start of the rains; fertiliser application (phosphate for legumes); weed control; fencing and allowing establishment before grazing
2 marks: (d) Any two, 1 mark each: legumes fix nitrogen, improving soil and grass growth; increase protein content of forage; improve palatability; provide a balanced diet
questions.explanation: Natural pasture grows unaided; artificial pasture is sown with selected species. Good grasses include Guinea and elephant grass; legumes include Centrosema and Stylosanthes. Establishment involves site selection, land preparation, choosing a mixture, sowing at the onset of rains, fertilising, weeding and fencing. Legumes fix nitrogen and raise protein content.

questions.stem:
(a) Distinguish between a crop disease and a crop pest. [2 marks]
(b) For each of the following diseases, name the type of causal organism, state two symptoms and one control measure: (i) black pod of cocoa; (ii) cassava mosaic disease; (iii) leaf spot (Cercospora) of groundnut. [12 marks]
(c) State four general effects of diseases on crop production. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) A disease is any condition that disturbs the normal functioning of a crop, caused by pathogens or adverse conditions; a pest is an animal that damages the crop directly by feeding, e.g. insects, rodents, birds
4 marks: (b)(i) Black pod: fungus (Phytophthora) (1 mark); symptoms: brown spots on pods spreading to cover whole pod; pod turns black and beans rot; white mould on pod (2 marks); control: remove/destroy infected pods, regular harvesting, spray copper fungicide, reduce shade (1 mark)
4 marks: (b)(ii) Cassava mosaic: virus (1 mark); symptoms: yellow/green mosaic patches on leaves; leaf distortion/curling; stunting; reduced tuber size (2 marks); control: plant resistant varieties or healthy cuttings, rogue infected plants, control whiteflies (1 mark)
4 marks: (b)(iii) Groundnut leaf spot: fungus (Cercospora) (1 mark); symptoms: brown or dark circular spots on leaves, often with yellow halo; premature leaf fall (2 marks); control: fungicide spray, crop rotation, resistant varieties, destroy crop residues (1 mark)
4 marks: (c) Any four, 1 mark each: reduce yield; lower quality and market value; increase cost of production; kill plants; reduce viability of seeds; make produce unfit/toxic for consumption
questions.explanation: A disease disrupts plant function and is caused by pathogens; a pest is an animal that feeds on crops. Black pod is caused by Phytophthora (fungus-like), blackening pods; control by removing infected pods and copper sprays. Cassava mosaic is a whitefly-borne virus causing mottled, distorted leaves; use clean cuttings and resistant varieties. Cercospora leaf spot causes dark spots and leaf fall; control by rotation and fungicides. Diseases lower yield and quality and raise costs.

questions.stem:
(a) Describe how a lawn can be established using grass runners (stolons). [6 marks]
(b) Explain four practices involved in maintaining a lawn. [8 marks]
(c) State four tools used in establishing and maintaining a lawn. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
6 marks: (a) Any three steps, 2 marks each: clear the site and remove stumps/stones; dig/till, level and rake the soil to a fine tilth, adding manure; plant runners/splits of a suitable grass (e.g. Cynodon, Paspalum, Axonopus) at close spacing at the onset of rains; water regularly until established; roll/firm the soil around runners
8 marks: (b) Any four explained, 2 marks each: mowing regularly to a uniform height; watering in the dry season; weeding/removal of broad-leaved weeds; fertiliser application to keep the lawn green; edging/trimming of borders; rolling to level the surface; pest and disease control; filling bare patches (re-planting)
4 marks: (c) Any four, 1 mark each: lawn mower; rake; shears/edging shears; watering can/hose/sprinkler; spade/garden fork; roller; wheelbarrow; cutlass
questions.explanation: A lawn is established by clearing, tilling, levelling and manuring the soil, planting runners of a lawn grass at the start of the rains, firming and watering. It is maintained by regular mowing, watering, weeding, fertilising, edging, rolling and patching. Tools include mowers, rakes, shears, hoses and rollers.

questions.stem:
(a) What is environmental physiology in livestock production? [2 marks]
(b) Explain how each of the following climatic factors affects farm animals: (i) high temperature; (ii) high relative humidity; (iii) rainfall; (iv) light (day length). [8 marks]
(c) State four ways of reducing heat stress in a poultry house. [4 marks]
(d) State four features that adapt indigenous cattle such as the White Fulani to hot climates. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) The study of how environmental (climatic) factors affect the body functions, growth, production and reproduction of farm animals
2 marks: (b)(i) Heat stress reduces feed intake, growth, milk and egg production; causes panting; lowers fertility
2 marks: (b)(ii) Reduces evaporative cooling (sweating/panting), increases heat stress; favours parasites and diseases; feed becomes mouldy
2 marks: (b)(iii) Determines the quantity and quality of pasture/water available; excessive rain causes wet housing and disease; drought causes feed shortage
2 marks: (b)(iv) Affects reproduction (onset of oestrus/laying in poultry); longer light increases egg production and feed intake
4 marks: (c) Any four, 1 mark each: good ventilation/open sides; orient house east-west; reduce stocking density; provide cool clean water; plant shade trees around house; roof insulation/reflective roofing; feed in cooler parts of the day; use fans/foggers
4 marks: (d) Any four, 1 mark each: large hump and dewlap (large surface area); loose skin; short, light-coloured coat; many sweat glands; tolerance of poor-quality feed; low metabolic rate; long legs
questions.explanation: Environmental physiology studies effects of climate on animal function. High temperature and humidity cause heat stress, reduced feed intake and output; rainfall controls feed supply and disease; light affects reproduction and laying. Ventilation, low stocking, shade, water and insulation reduce heat stress. Zebu cattle have humps, dewlaps, loose skin, light coats and many sweat glands.

questions.stem:
(a) What is artificial insemination (AI)? [2 marks]
(b) Describe the steps involved in carrying out artificial insemination in cattle. [8 marks]
(c) State four advantages and two disadvantages of artificial insemination. [6 marks]
(d) Name two materials or pieces of equipment used in AI. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) The deliberate introduction of semen collected from a selected male into the reproductive tract of a female in heat, by a trained person, without natural mating
2 marks: (b) Collection of semen from a superior bull using an artificial vagina
2 marks: (b) Evaluation of semen (motility, concentration) and dilution with extender
2 marks: (b) Storage/preservation in liquid nitrogen (frozen straws) and thawing before use
2 marks: (b) Detection of heat in the cow and deposition of semen into the cervix/uterus with an insemination gun at the right time
4 marks: (c) Advantages, any four, 1 mark each: one superior bull serves many cows; reduces cost of keeping bulls; prevents spread of venereal diseases; semen can be transported/stored for long; allows use of exotic genes without importing animals; allows mating of animals of different sizes
2 marks: (c) Disadvantages, any two, 1 mark each: requires skilled personnel; expensive equipment/liquid nitrogen; accurate heat detection needed; may spread disease if hygiene is poor; may reduce genetic diversity
2 marks: (d) Any two, 1 mark each: artificial vagina; insemination gun/catheter; liquid nitrogen flask; semen straws; microscope; speculum; gloves
questions.explanation: AI is placing semen from a chosen sire into a female in heat without mating. Semen is collected with an artificial vagina, evaluated, diluted, frozen in straws, thawed and deposited in the cervix with an insemination gun when the cow is on heat. AI spreads superior genes widely and cheaply and avoids venereal disease, but needs skill and equipment.

questions.stem:
(a) Name the three castes of honeybees in a colony and state one function of each. [6 marks]
(b) State four factors to consider in siting an apiary. [4 marks]
(c) Describe how honey is harvested from a Kenya top-bar hive. [5 marks]
(d) Name three products of beekeeping other than honey. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Queen: the only fertile female; lays eggs/produces pheromones that control the colony
2 marks: (a) Drones: fertile males; mate with the queen
2 marks: (a) Workers: sterile females; collect nectar and pollen, build comb, feed larvae, guard and clean the hive
4 marks: (b) Any four, 1 mark each: availability of flowering plants (forage); source of clean water nearby; shade and shelter from strong wind; away from human dwellings, roads and livestock; free from flooding; accessibility; security against theft and fire; away from heavy pesticide use
1 mark: (c) Harvest in the evening or early morning wearing protective clothing
1 mark: (c) Use a smoker to calm the bees
1 mark: (c) Open the hive and lift out the top bars with sealed (capped) honeycomb
1 mark: (c) Brush off bees and cut out the capped honeycomb, leaving brood comb and some honey for the colony
1 mark: (c) Place comb in a clean covered container and close the hive properly
3 marks: (d) Any three, 1 mark each: beeswax; propolis; royal jelly; pollen; bee venom; bee colonies (for sale)
questions.explanation: The queen lays eggs, drones mate with her and workers do all other work. Apiaries need forage, water, shade, distance from people and security. Honey is harvested at dusk or dawn with protective clothing and smoke, removing capped comb and leaving brood. Other products are beeswax, propolis, royal jelly and pollen.

questions.stem:
A farmer applied increasing numbers of bags of fertiliser to equal plots of maize. The yields were:
Bags of fertiliser: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
Yield (bags of maize): 20, 32, 42, 49, 53, 54
(a) State the law of diminishing returns. [3 marks]
(b) Calculate the marginal product (MP) of each additional bag of fertiliser from the 1st to the 5th bag. [5 marks]
(c) Calculate the average product per bag of fertiliser when 2 and 4 bags are applied, to two decimal places where necessary. [4 marks]
(d) At which bag of fertiliser does diminishing returns first become evident? [1 mark]
(e) If a bag of fertiliser costs N25 000 and a bag of maize sells for N40 000, should the farmer apply the 5th bag? Show your working. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a) When increasing quantities of a variable input are added to fixed inputs, the additional (marginal) output first increases but eventually declines, other things being equal
5 marks: (b) 1st: 32 - 20 = 12; 2nd: 10; 3rd: 7; 4th: 4; 5th: 1 bag of maize (1 mark each)
2 marks: (c) 2 bags: 42 / 2 = 21.00 bags of maize per bag of fertiliser
2 marks: (c) 4 bags: 53 / 4 = 13.25 bags of maize per bag of fertiliser
1 mark: (d) From the 2nd bag (MP falls from 12 to 10)
2 marks: (e) Value of MP of 5th bag = 1 x N40 000 = N40 000
2 marks: (e) Cost of 5th bag = N25 000; extra revenue (N40 000) exceeds extra cost (N25 000) by N15 000
1 mark: (e) Yes, the 5th bag is profitable to apply
questions.explanation: MP values are 12, 10, 7, 4 and 1 bags; average product at 2 bags is 42/2 = 21 and at 4 bags 53/4 = 13.25. MP declines from the 2nd bag, showing diminishing returns. The 5th bag adds 1 bag of maize worth N40 000 for a cost of N25 000, so it is still profitable.

questions.stem:
(a) Explain six problems faced by farm managers in Nigeria. [12 marks]
(b) Suggest one solution to each of three of the problems explained in (a). [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
12 marks: (a) Any six explained, 2 marks each: inadequate capital/credit; unpredictable weather; price fluctuations of produce and inputs; pests and diseases; shortage of skilled labour; poor infrastructure (roads, power, storage); land tenure problems; inadequate information/extension; insecurity (herder-farmer conflicts, theft); high cost of inputs; government policy changes
6 marks: (b) Any three appropriate solutions linked to stated problems, 2 marks each: e.g. access to cooperative/bank credit; agricultural insurance; irrigation; storage and processing to stabilise prices; integrated pest management; training of workers; government infrastructure provision; land reform; security measures
questions.explanation: Farm managers face shortage of capital, weather and price risks, pests, scarce skilled labour, poor infrastructure, land tenure issues, poor information, insecurity and high input costs. Remedies include credit through co-operatives, insurance, irrigation, storage, IPM, training and better infrastructure.

questions.stem:
(a) What is agricultural insurance? [2 marks]
(b) Explain the following terms: (i) premium; (ii) policy; (iii) indemnity. [6 marks]
(c) State four risks against which a farmer may insure. [4 marks]
(d) Give three reasons why many Nigerian farmers do not insure their farms, and three benefits of insurance to farmers. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) A scheme by which farmers pay regular contributions to an insurer in return for compensation if they suffer specified losses on their farms
2 marks: (b)(i) Premium: the periodic payment made by the insured farmer to the insurance company
2 marks: (b)(ii) Policy: the written contract/document stating the terms of the insurance
2 marks: (b)(iii) Indemnity: compensation that restores the insured to the financial position before the loss, not more
4 marks: (c) Any four, 1 mark each: fire; flood; drought; pest and disease outbreak; death of livestock; theft; storm/windstorm; accidents to farm machinery
3 marks: (d) Reasons, any three, 1 mark each: ignorance of insurance; high premiums; delays in paying claims; illiteracy; small farm size; distrust of insurance companies
3 marks: (d) Benefits, any three, 1 mark each: compensation for losses; encourages investment; makes it easier to get loans; reduces worry/uncertainty; promotes savings
questions.explanation: Agricultural insurance compensates farmers for specified losses in return for premiums. The premium is the regular payment, the policy is the contract, and indemnity restores the insured to the pre-loss position. Farmers insure against fire, flood, drought, disease, death of animals and theft. Many do not insure due to ignorance, cost and slow claims, though insurance aids credit and security.

questions.stem:
Describe the cultivation of cassava under the following headings:
(a) botanical name; [1 mark]
(b) climatic and soil requirements; [3 marks]
(c) land preparation; [2 marks]
(d) planting material and method of planting; [3 marks]
(e) spacing and plant population per hectare at the spacing stated; [3 marks]
(f) two cultural practices after planting; [2 marks]
(g) one disease and one pest, with a control method for each; [2 marks]
(h) harvesting and two processed products. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: (a) Manihot esculenta
3 marks: (b) Rainfall of about 1000-1500 mm; warm temperature (25-29 oC); well-drained loamy/sandy loam soil (1 mark each)
2 marks: (c) Clearing, ploughing and ridging or making mounds/heaps
3 marks: (d) Stem cuttings 20-25 cm long with 5-7 nodes from healthy mature stems (2 marks); planted slanting/vertical with two-thirds buried at start of rains (1 mark)
2 marks: (e) 1 m x 1 m (accept 1 m x 0.8 m etc.)
1 mark: (e) Population 10 000 plants per hectare (or correct value for spacing stated)
2 marks: (f) Any two, 1 mark each: weeding; fertiliser application (NPK); supplying (replacing failed cuttings); pest control
1 mark: (g) Disease: cassava mosaic disease (resistant varieties/clean cuttings) or bacterial blight
1 mark: (g) Pest: cassava mealybug (biological control) or green spider mite / variegated grasshopper
1 mark: (h) Harvest 9-18 months after planting by uprooting/digging out tubers
1 mark: (h) Any two products: garri; fufu/akpu; lafun; cassava flour; starch; tapioca
questions.explanation: Cassava (Manihot esculenta) needs warm, moderately wet conditions and well-drained loams. The land is cleared, ploughed and ridged; 20-25 cm stem cuttings are planted at the start of rains at 1 m x 1 m (10 000 plants per ha). Weeding, fertilising and supplying follow. Mosaic disease and mealybug are controlled by clean resistant material and biological control. Tubers are harvested after 9-18 months and processed into garri, fufu and flour.

questions.topic: Types and classification of farm animals
questions.stem:
(a) Classify farm animals according to their uses, giving two examples of each class. [8 marks]
(b) Give four differences between ruminants and non-ruminants. [4 marks]
(c) Name one indigenous breed each of (i) cattle; (ii) sheep; (iii) goat; and one exotic breed each of (iv) pig; (v) poultry (layer); (vi) dairy cattle. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Meat (beef/mutton/pork) animals, e.g. cattle, pigs, broilers, rabbits
2 marks: (a) Milk animals, e.g. dairy cattle (Friesian), goats
2 marks: (a) Egg producers, e.g. laying chickens, ducks, guinea fowl
2 marks: (a) Work/draught animals, e.g. bullocks, donkeys, horses, camels (accept fibre: sheep for wool; or pets/security: dogs)
4 marks: (b) Any four, 1 mark each: ruminants have a four-chambered stomach, non-ruminants a simple stomach; ruminants chew the cud, non-ruminants do not; ruminants digest cellulose with rumen microbes, non-ruminants poorly; ruminants lack upper incisors (dental pad), non-ruminants have them; ruminants feed mainly on roughage, non-ruminants on concentrates
6 marks: (c) 1 mark each: (i) White Fulani/N'Dama/Muturu/Red Bororo; (ii) Yankasa/Uda/Balami/West African Dwarf sheep; (iii) Red Sokoto/West African Dwarf/Sahel goat; (iv) Large White/Landrace/Duroc/Hampshire; (v) Isa Brown/Leghorn/Harco/Nera Black; (vi) Friesian/Jersey/Holstein/Guernsey
questions.explanation: Farm animals are grouped as meat, milk, egg, work and fibre animals. Ruminants have four stomach compartments, chew cud, digest cellulose and have a dental pad; non-ruminants have a simple stomach. Indigenous breeds include White Fulani cattle, Yankasa sheep and Red Sokoto goats; exotic breeds include Large White pigs, Isa Brown layers and Friesian dairy cattle.

questions.topic: Implications of demand and supply for agricultural production
questions.stem:
The table below shows the demand and supply schedules for beans in a market.
Price (N per kg): 200, 300, 400, 500, 600
Quantity demanded (kg): 900, 750, 600, 450, 300
Quantity supplied (kg): 300, 450, 600, 750, 900
(a) What is the equilibrium price and quantity? [2 marks]
(b) Calculate the shortage or surplus at (i) N300 per kg; (ii) N500 per kg. [4 marks]
(c) The government fixes a maximum price of N300 per kg. State three likely effects of this on the beans market. [3 marks]
(d) Explain three reasons why prices of farm produce fluctuate more than prices of manufactured goods. [6 marks]
(e) State three ways of stabilising prices of farm produce. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Equilibrium price N400 per kg; equilibrium quantity 600 kg (1 mark each)
2 marks: (b)(i) At N300: demand 750 kg, supply 450 kg; shortage of 300 kg
2 marks: (b)(ii) At N500: demand 450 kg, supply 750 kg; surplus of 300 kg
3 marks: (c) Any three, 1 mark each: shortage of 300 kg; black market/hoarding; queues/rationing; farmers reduce production; smuggling out to areas with higher prices
6 marks: (d) Any three explained, 2 marks each: seasonal production (glut at harvest, scarcity before harvest); perishability forces quick sale; weather and pests make output unpredictable; inelastic demand for food so small supply changes cause large price changes; long gestation of tree crops; poor storage facilities; many small producers with no control over price
3 marks: (e) Any three, 1 mark each: improved storage and processing; guaranteed minimum price/buffer stock schemes; marketing boards/co-operatives; irrigation for all-year production; better market information; commodity exchanges
questions.explanation: Demand equals supply at N400 per kg and 600 kg. At N300 there is a shortage of 750 - 450 = 300 kg; at N500 a surplus of 750 - 450 = 300 kg. A ceiling of N300 creates shortage, black markets and lower production. Farm prices fluctuate because of seasonality, perishability, weather, inelastic demand and poor storage; storage, buffer stocks, co-operatives and irrigation stabilise them.

questions.stem:
A sample of topsoil from a school farm in Ikom was put into a tall glass jar, water was added until the jar was three-quarters full, a pinch of salt (as dispersant) was added and the jar was shaken vigorously and left to stand for two days. The settled soil formed three distinct layers with a total height of 40 mm: bottom layer 22 mm (coarse, gritty particles); middle layer 10 mm (fine, smooth particles); top layer 8 mm (very fine, sticky particles). Some dark particles floated on the water surface.
(a) Name the particles in (i) the bottom layer; (ii) the middle layer; (iii) the top layer of the settled soil. [3 marks]
(b) Calculate the percentage by height of each of the three layers in the settled soil. [3 marks]
(c) Name the material floating on the water surface. [1 mark]
(d) Explain why the particles settled in layers. [2 marks]
(e) Using the result in (b), suggest the textural class of the soil. [1 mark]
(f) State two reasons why the jar was shaken vigorously. [2 marks]
(g) State three properties of the soil particles in the top layer that affect crop production. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a) (i) sand (gravel and sand); (ii) silt; (iii) clay (1 mark each)
3 marks: (b) Sand 22/40 x 100 = 55%; silt 10/40 x 100 = 25%; clay 8/40 x 100 = 20% (1 mark each)
1 mark: (c) Organic matter (humus/plant debris)
2 marks: (d) Particles settle according to size and weight; the largest/heaviest (sand) settle first and the finest (clay) settle last
1 mark: (e) Sandy clay loam (accept sandy loam/loam with valid reasoning)
2 marks: (f) To break the soil aggregates/separate particles; to mix the soil thoroughly with water
3 marks: (g) Any three, 1 mark each: high water-holding capacity; high nutrient retention (cation exchange); poor drainage/aeration when wet; sticky when wet and hard when dry; difficult to till
questions.explanation: The bottom layer is sand, then silt, then clay; floating material is organic matter. Percentages are 55% sand, 25% silt and 20% clay, giving a sandy clay loam. Heavier particles settle first. Shaking breaks aggregates. Clay holds water and nutrients but drains poorly and is hard to till.

questions.topic: Practical: Laboratory work on chemical properties of soil
questions.stem:
Soil samples were collected from three plots, P, Q and R, on a school farm. A 1:2.5 soil-water suspension of each was tested with a pH meter. The readings were: P - 4.6; Q - 6.8; R - 8.3.
(a) State whether each soil is acidic, neutral (near-neutral) or alkaline. [3 marks]
(b) Which of the plots is most suitable for growing most arable crops? Give a reason. [2 marks]
(c) Name one material that could be used to correct the condition of (i) plot P; (ii) plot R. [2 marks]
(d) An agronomist recommended 2.5 tonnes of agricultural lime per hectare for plot P, which measures 0.4 hectare. Calculate the quantity of lime required for plot P in kilograms. [3 marks]
(e) Apart from the pH meter, name two other materials that can be used to determine soil pH. [2 marks]
(f) State three effects of very low pH on crops. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a) P - acidic; Q - near-neutral (slightly acidic); R - alkaline (1 mark each)
1 mark: (b) Plot Q
1 mark: (b) Its pH (6.8) is within the range (about 6.0-7.0) in which most nutrients are available to crops
2 marks: (c) (i) P: lime (calcium carbonate/agricultural lime/dolomite/wood ash); (ii) R: gypsum/sulphur/organic matter/acid-forming fertiliser such as ammonium sulphate (1 mark each)
2 marks: (d) 2.5 t/ha x 0.4 ha = 1.0 tonne
1 mark: (d) = 1000 kg
2 marks: (e) Any two, 1 mark each: litmus paper; universal indicator solution/paper; soil pH test kit; BDH indicator
3 marks: (f) Any three, 1 mark each: phosphorus becomes unavailable (fixed); aluminium and manganese become toxic; reduced activity of nitrogen-fixing bacteria; deficiency of calcium and magnesium; poor root growth
questions.explanation: P (4.6) is acidic, Q (6.8) near-neutral and R (8.3) alkaline. Q is best because nutrients are most available near neutrality. Lime corrects acidity; gypsum or sulphur corrects alkalinity. Lime needed = 2.5 t/ha x 0.4 ha = 1.0 t = 1000 kg. Indicators and litmus can also show pH. Low pH causes P fixation, Al/Mn toxicity and poor microbial activity.

questions.stem:
A vegetable bed measuring 20 m by 15 m on a school farm in Kano needs 25 mm of water at each irrigation during the dry season. Students used 10-litre watering cans. (1 m3 = 1000 litres.)
(a) Calculate the area of the bed in square metres. [1 mark]
(b) Calculate the volume of water needed per irrigation (i) in cubic metres; (ii) in litres. [4 marks]
(c) How many full watering cans are required per irrigation? [2 marks]
(d) Suggest a more efficient irrigation method for the bed and give two reasons for your choice. [3 marks]
(e) State three factors that determine how often the bed should be irrigated. [3 marks]
(f) State two problems that may result from over-irrigation. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: (a) 20 m x 15 m = 300 m2
2 marks: (b)(i) 25 mm = 0.025 m; volume = 300 x 0.025 = 7.5 m3
2 marks: (b)(ii) 7.5 x 1000 = 7500 litres
2 marks: (c) 7500 / 10 = 750 cans
1 mark: (d) Drip (trickle) irrigation (accept sprinkler with reasons)
2 marks: (d) Any two, 1 mark each: saves water; reduces labour; supplies water directly to roots; reduces weed growth between rows; allows fertigation
3 marks: (e) Any three, 1 mark each: type of crop and stage of growth; soil type/water-holding capacity; temperature and evaporation rate; rainfall; wind; mulching
2 marks: (f) Any two, 1 mark each: waterlogging/poor aeration; leaching of nutrients; salinity build-up; erosion; root diseases; wastage of water
questions.explanation: Area = 300 m2; depth 0.025 m gives 7.5 m3 = 7500 L, i.e. 750 cans of 10 L. Drip irrigation saves water and labour. Frequency depends on crop, soil, evaporation and rainfall. Over-irrigation causes waterlogging, leaching and salinity.

questions.topic: Practical: Harvesting, processing and storage equipment
questions.stem:
Study the equipment described below.
Item A: a motorised machine with a hopper, a rotating drum with spikes and a sieve; maize cobs fed in come out as clean grains and separate cores.
Item B: a large cylindrical metal or concrete structure, airtight, with an opening at the top and a discharge outlet at the bottom, used to store grains in bulk.
Item C: a machine with a rotating drum covered with a perforated metal sheet with sharp edges, driven by an engine; peeled cassava tubers are fed into it.
Item D: a small curved blade on a wooden handle, sometimes with a serrated edge, used to cut rice or wheat stalks by hand.
Item E: a fan-driven machine into which threshed grain mixed with chaff is poured; the light chaff is blown away.
(a) Name each of items A to E. [5 marks]
(b) State one use of item C in food processing. [1 mark]
(c) State three conditions necessary for safe storage of grains in item B. [3 marks]
(d) State two maintenance practices for item A. [2 marks]
(e) State two advantages of using item E rather than traditional winnowing with a tray. [2 marks]
(f) Name one structure, other than item B, used for storing maize on the farm. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
5 marks: (a) A - maize sheller (thresher); B - silo; C - cassava grater; D - sickle; E - winnower (winnowing machine) (1 mark each)
1 mark: (b) Grating cassava into pulp/mash for garri or fufu production
3 marks: (c) Any three, 1 mark each: grains well dried (about 12-13% moisture); structure clean and fumigated/free of pests; airtight/protected from moisture; cool temperature; free from rodents
2 marks: (d) Any two, 1 mark each: clean after use; lubricate moving parts; check and tighten bolts/belts; service engine; store under shelter
2 marks: (e) Any two, 1 mark each: faster; cleaner grain; less labour; not dependent on wind
2 marks: (f) Crib / barn / rhumbu / store
questions.explanation: A is a maize sheller, B a silo, C a cassava grater, D a sickle and E a winnower. The grater produces cassava mash for garri. Silos need dry, clean, airtight, cool, pest-free conditions. Shellers should be cleaned and lubricated. Mechanical winnowers are faster and cleaner. Cribs and barns also store maize.

questions.stem:
The following parts of a farm tractor were pointed out to students:
Part F: a grid-like structure at the front of the engine filled with liquid, through which air is drawn by a fan.
Part G: a splined shaft at the rear of the tractor that rotates to drive machines such as rotavators and mowers.
Part H: three arms at the rear (two lower and one upper) to which implements are attached and lifted.
Part J: a box containing gears operated by a lever, which allows the operator to change speed and direction.
Part K: a container fitted with a removable element through which the engine draws in air.
(a) Name parts F, G, H, J and K. [5 marks]
(b) State the function of each of parts F and K. [2 marks]
(c) State two daily checks that should be carried out on part F and on the engine oil. [2 marks]
(d) State three safety precautions to observe when using part G. [3 marks]
(e) Name three implements that can be attached to part H. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
5 marks: (a) F - radiator; G - power take-off (PTO) shaft; H - three-point linkage (hitch); J - gearbox; K - air cleaner/air filter (1 mark each)
2 marks: (b) F: cools the engine by circulating water/coolant; K: removes dust from air entering the engine (1 mark each)
2 marks: (c) Check coolant/water level in the radiator and clean the radiator fins (1 mark); check engine oil level with dipstick and top up (1 mark)
3 marks: (d) Any three, 1 mark each: keep the PTO guard/shield in place; disengage PTO before getting down/making adjustments; avoid loose clothing near the rotating shaft; keep bystanders away; switch off the engine before attaching implements
3 marks: (e) Any three, 1 mark each: disc plough; disc harrow; ridger; rotavator (rotary tiller); boom sprayer; planter; mower; fertiliser broadcaster
questions.explanation: F is the radiator (cooling), G the PTO shaft, H the three-point linkage, J the gearbox and K the air cleaner (filters intake air). Daily checks include coolant and oil levels. Keep PTO guards on, avoid loose clothes and switch off before adjustment. Ploughs, harrows, ridgers and rotavators attach to the linkage.

questions.topic: Practical: Uses and maintenance of horticultural tools and implements
questions.stem:
Study the horticultural tools described below.
Tool L: a pair of short, strong, curved blades with spring-loaded handles, used with one hand.
Tool M: a pair of long, straight, flat blades with long wooden handles, used with two hands.
Tool N: a small sharp knife with a flat bone or plastic lip at the end of the handle.
Tool O: a rectangular metal container with a long spout ending in a perforated cap.
Tool P: a short-handled tool with a narrow, scoop-shaped metal blade.
(a) Name tools L to P. [5 marks]
(b) State one use of each of tools L, M, N, O and P. [5 marks]
(c) State three ways of maintaining tool N. [3 marks]
(d) Explain why the cap of tool O is perforated. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
5 marks: (a) L - secateurs (pruning shears); M - hedge shears (garden shears); N - budding knife; O - watering can; P - hand trowel (1 mark each)
5 marks: (b) L - pruning/cutting small branches and stems; M - trimming hedges and lawn edges; N - making cuts and lifting bark in budding/grafting; O - watering seedlings/nursery beds; P - lifting seedlings/transplanting/digging small holes (1 mark each)
3 marks: (c) Any three, 1 mark each: keep blade sharp; clean and disinfect after use; oil blade to prevent rust; fold/sheath and store in a dry place; use only for its purpose
2 marks: (d) The perforated rose breaks the water into fine droplets/spray so that it does not wash away soil or damage delicate seedlings
questions.explanation: L is secateurs (pruning), M hedge shears (trimming hedges), N a budding knife (budding and grafting), O a watering can and P a hand trowel. The budding knife must be kept sharp, clean, oiled and stored dry. The perforated rose gives a gentle spray that protects seedlings and soil.

questions.topic: Practical: Planting dates, seed rates, plant population and seed quality tests
questions.stem:
A farmer intends to plant 1 hectare of cowpea at a spacing of 60 cm x 30 cm with two seeds per hole. A germination test on the seed lot gave 80% germination. A sample of 100 seeds weighed 20 g.
(a) Calculate the number of planting holes per hectare. [3 marks]
(b) Calculate the number of seeds required, assuming every hole is sown. [2 marks]
(c) Calculate the mass of seed required in kilograms, to one decimal place. [3 marks]
(d) Adjust the seed requirement in (c) for 80% germination, to one decimal place. [2 marks]
(e) Describe how the germination test could have been carried out using a Petri dish. [3 marks]
(f) State two reasons why planting date is important in cowpea production. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: (a) Area per hole = 0.6 m x 0.3 m = 0.18 m2
2 marks: (a) Holes = 10 000 / 0.18 = 55 556 (55 555.6)
2 marks: (b) Seeds = 2 x 55 556 = 111 111 (accept 111 112)
1 mark: (c) Mass per seed = 20 / 100 = 0.2 g
2 marks: (c) Mass = 111 111 x 0.2 = 22 222 g = 22.2 kg
2 marks: (d) 22.2 / 0.8 = 27.8 kg
3 marks: (e) Place moist cotton wool/filter paper in a Petri dish; arrange a counted number (e.g. 100) of seeds on it; keep moist at room temperature; count germinated seeds after about 5-7 days and express as a percentage (any three steps, 1 mark each)
2 marks: (f) Any two, 1 mark each: ensures adequate moisture for germination and growth; avoids peak pest periods (e.g. pod borers); ensures harvesting in dry weather to avoid pod rot; makes use of the full growing season
questions.explanation: Holes = 10 000 / (0.6 x 0.3) = 55 556; seeds = 111 111; at 0.2 g per seed this is 22.2 kg, adjusted to 22.2 / 0.8 = 27.8 kg for 80% germination. A Petri dish test uses moist paper and a counted sample. Timing planting ensures moisture, avoids pests and allows dry-season harvest.

questions.topic: Practical: Seedbed preparation and crop husbandry operations
questions.stem:
A class prepared a vegetable seedbed and raised tomato seedlings for transplanting. The operations carried out (not in order) were: harrowing; transplanting; clearing; hardening-off; ploughing; nursery sowing; mulching.
(a) Arrange the operations in the correct order. [3 marks]
(b) Name one tool or implement for each of: (i) clearing; (ii) ploughing on a small plot; (iii) transplanting. [3 marks]
(c) What is hardening-off and why is it done? [3 marks]
(d) State three precautions to observe when transplanting seedlings. [3 marks]
(e) State three benefits of mulching the seedbed. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a) Clearing, ploughing, harrowing, nursery sowing, hardening-off, transplanting, mulching (accept nursery sowing earlier, provided field sequence is correct; deduct 1 mark per error)
3 marks: (b) (i) cutlass/machete; (ii) hoe/garden fork/spade; (iii) hand trowel (1 mark each)
1 mark: (c) Gradual exposure of nursery seedlings to field conditions (full sun, reduced watering)
2 marks: (c) To toughen seedlings so that they survive transplanting shock in the field
3 marks: (d) Any three, 1 mark each: water the nursery before lifting; transplant in the evening or on a cloudy day; lift with a ball of soil around roots; select healthy, vigorous seedlings; water immediately after transplanting; plant at the correct depth and spacing
3 marks: (e) Any three, 1 mark each: conserves soil moisture; suppresses weeds; reduces erosion; moderates soil temperature; adds organic matter as it decays
questions.explanation: The order is clearing, ploughing, harrowing, nursery sowing, hardening-off, transplanting, mulching. A cutlass clears, a hoe or fork digs, a trowel transplants. Hardening-off gradually exposes seedlings to field conditions to reduce shock. Transplant in the cool of the day with soil around roots and water well. Mulch conserves moisture, suppresses weeds and controls erosion.

questions.stem:
Study the forest products described below.
Specimen Q: a sawn plank of reddish-brown hardwood, heavy and durable, obtained from a tall rainforest tree.
Specimen R: a thick, sticky, milky fluid that hardens on exposure to air, collected in cups from slanting cuts on a tree trunk.
Specimen S: black, light, brittle lumps that burn without flame and give intense heat, sold in sacks along highways.
Specimen T: a golden, sweet, viscous liquid collected from wild colonies in hollow trees.
Specimen U: thin, flexible strips from the leaf stalks of a palm, used to make baskets and furniture.
(a) Identify specimens Q to U. [5 marks]
(b) Name one tree species from which specimen Q may be obtained. [1 mark]
(c) Name the tree from which specimen R is obtained and one product made from it. [2 marks]
(d) Briefly describe how specimen S is produced. [3 marks]
(e) State two harmful effects of uncontrolled production of specimen S on the forest. [2 marks]
(f) State two other non-timber forest products. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
5 marks: (a) Q - timber (hardwood plank); R - latex; S - charcoal; T - honey; U - cane/rattan (raffia strips accepted) (1 mark each)
1 mark: (b) Any one: mahogany (Khaya); iroko (Milicia excelsa); obeche (Triplochiton); African walnut; opepe; afara
2 marks: (c) Rubber tree (Hevea brasiliensis) (1 mark); tyres/shoes/gloves/rubber bands/foam (1 mark)
3 marks: (d) Wood is stacked and covered with earth/placed in a kiln; burnt slowly with limited air supply (pyrolysis); cooled and the charcoal removed (1 mark each)
2 marks: (e) Any two, 1 mark each: deforestation; loss of biodiversity/wildlife habitat; soil erosion; bush fires; climate change
2 marks: (f) Any two, 1 mark each: bush mango (ogbono); chewing sticks; snails; bush meat; mushrooms; medicinal plants; gum arabic; kola; shea nuts; locust bean
questions.explanation: Q is hardwood timber (e.g. mahogany, iroko), R latex from the rubber tree used for tyres, S charcoal, T honey and U rattan cane. Charcoal is made by burning wood slowly with limited air. Uncontrolled charcoal production causes deforestation and erosion. Other NTFPs include bush mango, snails and medicinal plants.

questions.stem:
Study the animal by-products described below.
Specimen V: a brownish, dry, odourless powder obtained by drying and grinding coagulated blood from an abattoir.
Specimen W: a whitish-grey powder from heated, crushed animal bones.
Specimen X: tanned, flexible material made from the skin of a goat.
Specimen Y: dried dung and urine mixed with bedding from a cattle pen.
Specimen Z: hard, curved, hollow structures removed from the head of a ram.
(a) Identify specimens V to Z. [5 marks]
(b) State the main nutrient supplied by (i) specimen V; (ii) specimen W in livestock feed. [2 marks]
(c) State two uses of specimen X. [2 marks]
(d) State two ways in which specimen Y improves soil. [2 marks]
(e) State one use of specimen Z. [1 mark]
(f) State three precautions in processing specimen V to make it safe for use in feed. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
5 marks: (a) V - blood meal; W - bone meal; X - leather; Y - farmyard manure; Z - horns (1 mark each)
2 marks: (b) (i) protein (lysine); (ii) calcium and phosphorus (minerals) (1 mark each)
2 marks: (c) Any two, 1 mark each: shoes; bags; belts; drums; upholstery; book binding
2 marks: (d) Any two, 1 mark each: adds nutrients; improves soil structure; increases water-holding capacity; increases microbial activity
1 mark: (e) Making buttons, combs, ornaments, horn meal, musical instruments (horns/trumpets)
3 marks: (f) Any three, 1 mark each: collect blood hygienically; heat/cook thoroughly to kill pathogens; dry completely to prevent spoilage; store in a dry, clean container; avoid blood from diseased animals
questions.explanation: V is blood meal (protein), W bone meal (Ca and P), X leather, Y farmyard manure and Z horns. Leather makes shoes and bags; manure supplies nutrients and improves structure; horns make buttons and combs. Blood meal must be hygienically collected, cooked and dried.

questions.topic: Practical: Animal feeds and feed stuffs
questions.stem:
A group of 50 broiler chickens was fed for one week. At the start of the week the birds weighed 40.0 kg altogether, and at the end they weighed 50.0 kg. During the week they ate 21.0 kg of feed. The feed was compounded from maize, soya bean meal, fish meal, wheat offal, bone meal, oyster shell, salt and vitamin-mineral premix.
(a) Calculate (i) the total weight gain of the flock; (ii) the average weight gain per bird. [3 marks]
(b) Calculate the feed conversion ratio (FCR) for the week. [2 marks]
(c) What does an FCR of this value mean? [1 mark]
(d) Classify the feed ingredients listed into energy sources, protein sources and mineral/vitamin sources. [6 marks]
(e) State three factors that may cause a poor (high) feed conversion ratio. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a)(i) 50.0 - 40.0 = 10.0 kg
1 mark: (a)(ii) 10.0 / 50 = 0.2 kg (200 g) per bird
2 marks: (b) FCR = feed eaten / weight gain = 21.0 / 10.0 = 2.1
1 mark: (c) The birds needed 2.1 kg of feed to gain 1 kg of live weight
2 marks: (d) Energy: maize, wheat offal
2 marks: (d) Protein: soya bean meal, fish meal
2 marks: (d) Minerals/vitamins: bone meal, oyster shell, salt, premix (all four for 2 marks, two or three for 1 mark)
3 marks: (e) Any three, 1 mark each: poor-quality/unbalanced feed; disease or parasites; feed wastage; heat stress; poor breed/genetic potential; overcrowding; inadequate water
questions.explanation: The flock gained 10.0 kg, i.e. 0.2 kg per bird. FCR = 21.0 / 10.0 = 2.1, meaning 2.1 kg of feed per kg of gain. Maize and wheat offal supply energy, soya and fish meal protein, and bone meal, oyster shell, salt and premix minerals and vitamins. Poor feed, disease, wastage, heat stress and poor genetics raise FCR.

questions.topic: Practical: Main pests and diseases of crops
questions.stem:
Study the diseased plant specimens described below.
Specimen A: cocoa pods with brown, spreading patches that later turn the whole pod black; a whitish powdery growth appears on the surface in wet weather.
Specimen B: maize leaves with narrow, broken, pale-yellow streaks running parallel to the veins; the plant is stunted.
Specimen C: groundnut plants with small, crowded, yellowish or dark green leaves forming a bushy, dwarfed plant.
Specimen D: cowpea leaves with brown, sunken spots that later merge, and dark lesions on stems and pods.
(a) Name the disease shown by each of specimens A to D. [4 marks]
(b) Name the type of causal organism of (i) specimen A; (ii) specimen B. [2 marks]
(c) Name the vector of the disease in (i) specimen B; (ii) specimen C. [2 marks]
(d) State one control measure for each of specimens A, B and C. [3 marks]
(e) State four general ways in which crop diseases spread. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: (a) A - black pod disease; B - maize streak; C - groundnut rosette; D - anthracnose (brown blotch accepted) (1 mark each)
2 marks: (b) (i) fungus (Phytophthora); (ii) virus (1 mark each)
2 marks: (c) (i) leafhopper (Cicadulina); (ii) aphid (Aphis craccivora) (1 mark each)
3 marks: (d) A: regular removal of infected pods/copper fungicide spray/reduce shade; B: resistant varieties/early planting/control leafhoppers; C: early planting at close spacing/resistant varieties/control aphids (1 mark each)
4 marks: (e) Any four, 1 mark each: wind; water splash/rain; insects and other vectors; infected planting materials/seeds; contaminated tools; humans and animals; soil
questions.explanation: A is black pod (Phytophthora), B maize streak (virus, leafhopper vector), C groundnut rosette (virus, aphid vector) and D anthracnose. Controls include removing infected pods and copper sprays, resistant varieties and early planting. Diseases spread by wind, water, vectors, infected planting material, tools and soil.
